messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Daniel, a 45-year-old European American journalist, came to treatment after nearly a year of feeling as though his body and mind no longer belonged to him in the way they once had. Before the trauma, he had built his life around deadlines, interviews, and the ordinary unpredictability of reporting. Then, while on assignment abroad, he was taken captive and held against his will. He did not speak about every detail at first, but in the way he described it, the experience had been defined by confinement, physical control, and the constant sense that anything around him might turn dangerous without warning. He remembered being grabbed and restrained, his neck aching from the way he had been handled, the feeling of another person’s hands on him, and the sharp, unmistakable smell of alcohol in the room where he was kept. Those impressions had become fixed in him with unusual force.

In the months after he returned home, Daniel found that certain moments could drop him back into that period with little warning. Neck pain, even when it came from something ordinary like sleeping awkwardly or sitting too long at his desk, would make him tense immediately. What started as a physical discomfort could suddenly feel loaded, as if the ache itself were a signal that something bad was happening again. Physical touch was especially hard for him. He had been married for many years, and he cared deeply about his wife, but even a brief touch on the shoulder or an unexpected hand on his arm could make him pull away before he had time to think. He would often apologize afterward, but he could see how puzzling it was to her that something so small could make him flinch so hard.

The smell of alcohol was another powerful cue. Daniel noticed it most vividly in ordinary public places: passing someone near a bar after work, entering a restaurant with a crowded happy hour, or standing close to a person who had been drinking. The smell did not simply remind him of the captivity; it seemed to bring the whole scene back at once. He would become rigid, his attention narrowing to whatever was around him, and for a moment he would behave as if he were back in the place where he had been held. He described this as reacting before he had a chance to decide what was happening. At times he would know, even in the middle of a perfectly safe street or office corridor, that nothing was actually wrong, yet his body would have already moved into alarm.

Loud or unexpected sounds became difficult to tolerate. In the newsroom, where phones rang, chairs scraped, and voices rose without much notice, Daniel found himself constantly on edge. A dropped mug, a slammed door, or a sudden burst of laughter from another room could make him feel instantly exposed. He was not simply startled in the usual way; he became high alert, watching the room as if expecting the next sound to tell him something important about danger. He began sitting with his back to the wall when he could, scanning entrances without thinking, and staying alert even during routine conversations. This state of being superwatchful was exhausting, but he felt he could not afford to let his guard down.

The memories themselves had become one of the most distressing parts of his life. Daniel said it felt as though the event played like a film on repeat, not in a way that he chose, but as if the scene imposed itself on him. He could be in the middle of editing copy, helping with dinner, or trying to fall asleep, and the memory would force its way into his mind when he did not want it there. When it came, it did not feel like a distant recollection. Remembering brought back the same terror he had felt at the time, with the same tight chest, the same sense that he had to stay alert to survive. He had become careful about what he watched, what he listened to, and where he sat in a room, because he never knew what might set off the replay.

Over time, these experiences affected how Daniel moved through daily life. He became less willing to linger in crowded places after work, and he began avoiding situations where alcohol would be part of the environment. He also noticed that he was less present with his wife in ordinary physical affection, which weighed on him because their marriage had always been a source of stability. At work, he still met deadlines and tried to function as the journalist he had always been, but colleagues noticed he seemed more watchful and harder to startle than before. He had come to feel that something in him remained stuck in the captivity, as if his body kept expecting the next unexpected sound, the next touch, the next reminder in the air.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was no longer only worried about the memories themselves, but about how much of his life had become organized around anticipating them. He hoped therapy might help him feel safe again in his own body, in his marriage, and at work, and what frightened him most was the sense that if this continued, he might remain forever braced for a danger that was no longer there.
